newsitem.title: USA: U.S. blue chips fall as interest rates jump.
newsitem.headline: U.S. blue chips fall as interest rates jump.

text.p: Stocks slumped on Friday as investors, lulled by recent signs of mild inflation, were shocked by surprisingly strong reports on U.S. employment and manufacturing activity.
But the stock market again proved its resilience, shaking off most of the day's drop to end with moderate losses, even as bonds failed to recover from a sharp sell-off.
By the end, the session appeared to represent little more than a breather for the stock market, with the Dow Jones industrial average falling 28.57 points to 8,194.04.
In the broader market, decliners beat advancers 1,827 to 1,043 on volume of 511.6 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange. Weekly volume totalled 2.6 billion shares.

The late recovery all but erased an early sell-off that dragged the Dow down as much as 120 points, but even so, analysts pointed to the heavy early losses as evidence the market is ill-prepared to withstand any unpleasant surprises
The first surprise, which triggered a freefall in the bond market, was the Labour Department's report that the economy added 316,000 new jobs in July, far outpacing forecasts for about 200,000.
A second report showed U.S. manufacturing activity and prices paid by manufacturers both registered unexpectedly sharp rises, reawakening latent inflation concerns.
Investors immediately engaged in a broad selling spree after the news, intent on cashing in on some of the market's dizzying and relentless gains.

"The image I use is that of a forest that hasn't experienced a fire in a very long time," said Charlie Crane, chief market strategist at Key Asset Management. "You get one spark and suddenly you have a blaze on your hands."
Analysts were reluctant to predict whether the market was destined to duplicate last summer's performance, when stocks corrected steeply after a similar employment report surprise.
But several analysts said the market appeared to have little room to manoeuvre higher, if only because investors have already built an ideal outlook into pricing levels.

The reports also threw a scare into the inflation-sensitive bond market, where the bellwether 30-year Treasury plunged 2-1/32, or $20.3125 on a $1,000 bond, pushing its yield to 6.45 percent from 6.30 percent at Thursday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
"Both the bond and stock markets have come a very long way," said Gail Dudack, chief investment strategist at UBS Securities.
"What today says is that both markets are in the process of discounting perfection," she said, "and when you do get a blemish, the result is a sharp retracement."
The retracement hit interest rate-sensitive shares particularly hard and sent bank stocks tumbling.
Bank of New York Co. Inc. fell 1-7/16 to 47-3/16 and BankAmerica Corp shed 1-3/8 to 74-1/8. Dow component J.P. Morgan & Co. Inc. fell 1-3/8 to 114-1/2.

Among other issues, Kellogg Co. jumped 5-9/16 to 97-7/16 after the company's second-quarter earnings more than doubled, coming in well ahead of Wall Street estimates. The company also raised its dividend and declared a stock split.

Kenneth Cole Productions Inc. fell 2-3/4 to 12-1/2 after the fashion shoe company reported second-quarter net income fell 70 percent from a year ago and Morgan Stanley lowered its rating on the shares to neutral.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks fell 7.15 points to 947.14. The Nasdaq Composite rose 0.52 to a record 1,594.33.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues, also known as the Wilshire 5,000 -- ended at 8.977.584, down 53.843, or 0.60 percent.
